title: Netherlands Returns 1,000-Year-Old Chola Copper Plates to India After 14-Year Diplomatic Campaign
excerpt: The Anaimangalam inscriptions, among the most significant surviving records of Rajaraja Chola I's reign, were formally repatriated from Leiden University during Prime Minister Modi's visit to The Hague.
body:
The Netherlands on Friday formally returned the 11th-century Anaimangalam copper plates to India, concluding a 14-year diplomatic effort to reclaim one of the most important pieces of Tamil heritage held outside the country. The repatriation coincided with Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to The Hague as part of a five-nation European and Asian tour.

The artefacts — 21 large and three small copper sheets weighing nearly 30 kilograms, bound together by a circular copper ring carrying the royal Chola seal — date to the reign of Emperor Rajaraja Chola I (985-1014 CE) and are widely regarded as among the most significant surviving records of the Chola dynasty's administration, diplomacy and cultural reach.

What the Plates Reveal

Known in the Netherlands as the Leiden Plates, the inscriptions document grants of land revenues and taxes to the Chudamani Vihara, a Buddhist monastery in Nagapattinam, Tamil Nadu, built by Sri Mara Vijayotunga Varman, the ruler of the Srivijaya kingdom in present-day Indonesia. While Rajaraja Chola I issued the original grant, his son, Emperor Rajendra Chola I, later had the order engraved onto durable copper plates to ensure its permanent preservation.

Historians say the inscriptions provide rare insight into the maritime trade networks, religious pluralism and cultural exchanges that connected South India and Southeast Asia at the height of Chola power. The records demonstrate how Hindu rulers of the era patronised Buddhist institutions — a tradition of religious coexistence that scholars describe as central to understanding medieval Indian civilisation.

"These are not merely administrative documents," historians note. "They are windows into the cosmopolitan and commercially connected world of medieval South India."

How They Ended Up in the Netherlands

The plates were removed from India during Dutch colonial rule on the Coromandel Coast in the 18th century. Historians believe they were acquired by Dutch official Florentius Camper through a Christian missionary operating in the region, at a time when the Dutch East India Company controlled Nagapattinam — having moved its Coromandel headquarters there from Pulicat in 1690.

The artefacts entered the collection of Leiden University in 1862 through the estate of Professor Hendrik Arent Hamaker and remained housed in the university library's secured vaults, accessible mainly to researchers through advance requests. They were widely studied by Tamil epigraphists and also entered popular culture through Ponniyin Selvan, the celebrated Tamil historical novel set during the Chola era.

The Restitution Breakthrough

India had long pursued the return of the plates through diplomatic channels. The breakthrough came after the Netherlands finalised a national restitution policy for colonial-era artefacts in 2022, which created a framework for evaluating and returning objects removed without consent. Detailed provenance research by the Independent Colonial Collections Committee and Leiden University Libraries concluded that the inscriptions should be repatriated.

The return is part of a broader global movement to reclaim colonial-era artefacts. The Netherlands has also repatriated objects to Sri Lanka and Indonesia in recent years, while the United States recently announced the return of over 1,400 antiquities valued at $10 million to India.

Why This Matters to the Diaspora

For the large Tamil diaspora in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Singapore and Malaysia, the Chola dynasty holds a special place in cultural identity. The Brihadisvara Temple in Thanjavur, built by Rajaraja Chola I, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most visited landmarks for heritage-conscious NRIs. The return of the Anaimangalam plates — tangible links to that golden age — has been welcomed as both a diplomatic achievement and a symbolic restoration of cultural memory.

What's Next

The copper plates will be transferred to the Archaeological Survey of India and are expected to be displayed in Tamil Nadu. The repatriation adds momentum to India's growing campaign to recover stolen and colonial-era artefacts held in institutions across Europe and North America — a campaign that has accelerated under the Modi government and now encompasses hundreds of objects recovered from dozens of countries.
